title: Turn a List Around
statement:
You get the head of a singly linked list. Reverse it so that the last node comes first, and return the new head.

Reverse the links between the existing nodes. Each node should end up pointing at the node that used to come before it.

Lists in the tests are written as arrays: [4, 9, 2] is the list 4 → 9 → 2. An empty list is null (shown as [] in examples).

examples.why: Every arrow flips: 4 → 9 → 2 → 7 becomes 7 → 2 → 9 → 4, and the old tail 7 is the new head.
One node has no links to flip. Its next is still null.
The empty list reversed is still empty. Return null, not a dummy node.

hints: Walk the list once. When you stand on a node, which pointer do you want to change, and what do you lose if you change it right away?
Before you overwrite cur.next, save it somewhere. Otherwise the rest of the list is gone.
Keep two pointers: prev (the already reversed part, starting at null) and cur. Save next, point cur.next at prev, then move both one step.

explain.intuition:
Think of the list as a row of people, each pointing at the person to their right. To reverse the row, everyone turns to point left. You can do that walking left to right, one person at a time, as long as you remember who was on the right before you turn the current person around. That saved pointer is the whole trick.

At every moment the list is split in two: a reversed part that starts at prev, and the untouched part that starts at cur. Each step moves one node from the second part to the front of the first. When cur runs off the end, prev is the old tail, which is the new head.
steps: While cur is not null: save nxt = cur.next.
Return prev. For an empty list it is null, which is correct.
pitfalls: Overwriting cur.next before saving it. The loop then jumps back into the reversed part and stops after one node.
Returning head at the end. The old head is now the tail; the new head is prev.
Writing it recursively in Python. With 50 000 nodes the recursion goes 50 000 calls deep, far past Python's default limit of about 1000.

solutions.title: Copy values, rebuild backwards
solutions.idea: Read the values into an array, then build a fresh list from the end of the array. Easy to get right, but it allocates n new nodes instead of relinking the old ones.

solutions.title: Flip pointers in one pass
solutions.idea: Keep the reversed part in prev and the rest in cur. Save cur.next, point cur back at prev, then step forward.

followups: Write it recursively. What does each call return, and when is the recursion depth a problem?
Reverse only the nodes from position left to position right, leaving the rest in place.
